name: Graham net-nets
summary: Companies priced at two-thirds or less of their net current asset value. Expect a short list.
how_to_read: One filter: net current asset value (current assets minus all liabilities) of at least 1.5× market cap. That is Graham's test of a price at or below two-thirds of NCAV. Few companies pass, and a short list here is expected, not an error. The names that do pass are usually tiny and thinly traded: check average dollar volume before reading anything into the list. A market cap that looks implausibly small next to the daily trading volume usually means a share-count error in the inputs, so open the company and check the share count. Glint shows the list. It doesn't test or claim any returns.
misses: What current assets would fetch in a sale: NCAV takes them at book value, and inventory or receivables may be worth far less.
Cash burn: a net-net that loses money every quarter can see its NCAV shrink quickly.
Most foreign filers: they have no market cap yet (price ratios need currency conversion and ADR ratios), so they don't appear.
source: Graham and Dodd, Security Analysis (1934); Graham, The Intelligent Investor (1949)
